clue.text: What Clint Smoker says he does for work in Shanghai

parts.note: Clint Smoker, the tabloid hack in Martin Amis's Yellow Dog, introduces himself with I'm, short for I am
his trade is journalism, the press

explanation.surface: A question about a fictional journalist's job somewhere in China.
explanation.walkthrough: Shanghai looks like the city, but it is the verb: to force someone into service, as press gangs did with sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: To shanghai a sailor was to force him aboard, just as press gangs would compel men into naval service.

clue.text: Iranian novel about Kelvin North, a crime writer

indicators.note: about places the anagram around the two abbreviations
novel means new, so the letters of Iranian are given a new arrangement

parts.note: K is the symbol for kelvin, the unit of temperature

explanation.surface: A Persian novel is about a man called Kelvin North and a detective writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' rearranges IRANIAN into IANRAIN, and 'about' puts NK inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish author of the Inspector Rebus novels is a leading writer of crime fiction.

clue.text: Retro T-shirt perhaps and cape for Doc Sportello?

indicators.note: retro means backward-looking, so the garment word is read in reverse

parts.note: a T-shirt is an example of a top
a head is a headland or cape

explanation.surface: A vintage T-shirt and a cloak are the costume for a Pynchon private eye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retro' turns TOP into POT. Doc Sportello, hero of Pynchon's Inherent Vice, is a pot-smoking private eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Pynchon's detective is a habitual cannabis smoker, so he is an example of a stoner.

clue.text: Morse code ultimately drove UN nuts, article admitted

indicators.note: ultimately picks the last letter of the word code
admitted puts the article inside the anagram
nuts means crazy, so the letters of drove UN are jumbled

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Morse code is used to send messages to the United Nations.
explanation.walkthrough: Morse code reads as one phrase, but Morse alone is the definition. 'nuts' rearranges DROVEUN into NDEVOUR, and 'admitted' puts A inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspector Morse's first name is this, and the prequel series about him is named after it.

clue.text: Tobermory was his cat as a kitten for a while

indicators.note: for a while says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A man recalls owning a cat named Tobermory when it was young.
explanation.walkthrough: Tobermory is the talking cat in a short story by this Edwardian writer, the pen name of H. H. Munro.
explanation.definitionFit: The writer H. H. Munro, who used this pen name, wrote the short story Tobermory about a talking cat.

clue.text: Actor brought back food for Prof Lidenbrock's home

parts.note: a ham is an overacting performer

indicators.note: brought back tells us the word for food is read from right to left

parts.note: grub is slang for food

explanation.surface: A performer returns with a meal for a professor from a Jules Verne novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought back' turns GRUB into BURG. Professor Lidenbrock, of Verne's Journey to the Centre of the Earth, lives in this German port city.
explanation.definitionFit: Verne's geologist Otto Lidenbrock keeps his house and study in the north German port city.

clue.text: One hoping to get a lift in Ford Prefect?

definitions.text: One hoping to get a lift in Ford Prefect?

parts.words: One hoping to get a lift in Ford Prefect?
parts.note: reads as someone wanting a ride in an old Ford car, but Ford Prefect is the alien thumbing rides across the galaxy in Douglas Adams's comic novel

explanation.walkthrough: The Ford Prefect was a British family car; Douglas Adams named his alien traveller after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ford Prefect travels the galaxy by thumbing rides on passing spaceships, so he is a lift-seeker.

clue.text: Playwright encountered around Palma regularly

indicators.note: around puts the first piece outside the letters picked from Palma

parts.note: met means encountered

indicators.note: regularly picks every other letter of the word Palma

explanation.surface: A dramatist meets someone on Majorca.
explanation.walkthrough: Palma regularly gives AM, the second and fourth letters.
explanation.definitionFit: David Mamet is an American dramatist, author of Glengarry Glen Ross.

clue.text: You might say Becky Sharp is out of bed by dawn

parts.note: someone up is out of bed
dawn means the beginning, or start

explanation.surface: Thackeray's heroine is said to rise early.
explanation.walkthrough: Becky Sharp, the scheming heroine of Thackeray's Vanity Fair, climbs society from humble beginnings.
explanation.definitionFit: Becky Sharp is a social climber who rises above her station, the classic example of an arriviste.

clue.text: In which top Kurt Janisch is first to grill grass

definitions.text: In which top Kurt Janisch is

indicators.note: first to picks the opening letter of the word grill

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass

explanation.surface: A policeman in a novel is the first to question someone about drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: Kurt Janisch is the police officer at the centre of Elfriede Jelinek's novel of this title.
explanation.definitionFit: Jelinek's 2000 novel Gier, published in English under this title, has Kurt Janisch as its lead character.

clue.text: Widely-known books found in west facing study

indicators.note: found in places the books inside the other piece of wordplay
in an across answer, facing west means pointing leftwards, so the word for study is read backwards

parts.note: a den is a private study
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: Famous books turn up in a study that looks westward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'west facing' makes NED; in a down or across grid, west means right-to-left, the direction of reading backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Something widely known is celebrated or famous, a common sense of the adjective.

clue.text: Model given audio casting for Labyrinth producer

indicators.note: an audio casting is a version heard rather than seen, so the model's name is turned into a word with that sound

parts.note: Kate Moss is a famous British fashion model

explanation.surface: A model has a voice part in a fantasy film called Labyrinth.
explanation.walkthrough: Labyrinth suggests the Jim Henson film, but here it is the 2005 novel of that name; its author's name is said just like the model's.
explanation.definitionFit: The bestselling 2005 novel Labyrinth was written by the English author with this name.

clue.text: A cross bloke snorting drug in American Psycho?

indicators.note: snorting puts the drug right at the bloke's nose, at his front

parts.note: X is the shape of a cross
E is the abbreviation for ecstasy
a bloke is a man

explanation.surface: An angry man takes cocaine, like the yuppie killer of Bret Easton Ellis's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Cross looks like 'angry', but it is the letter X.
explanation.definitionFit: Patrick Bateman, the American Psycho, kills with an axe, so the question mark marks him as an example of a hatchet killer.

clue.text: Small film network in HD shows crime series

indicators.note: in places the film and network inside the two letters HD

parts.note: ET is the Spielberg film
LAN is a local area network

explanation.surface: A TV channel's high-definition service carries a crime drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The BBC crime drama is set on the Scottish islands and named after them.

clue.text: "is true friendship" (William Blake)

parts.note: the missing word starts the proverb in Blake's The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, saying enmity is a better friend than flattery

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the gap is the first word of Blake's saying.
explanation.definitionFit: Blake's saying holds that resistance and disagreement are worth more than agreement among friends.

clue.text: I would party with one in front of Kentish lad

indicators.note: one in front of asks for the single letter at the very front of the word Kentish

parts.note: I'd is short for I would
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Someone wants to celebrate with a boy from Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: Kentish lad sounds like a regional phrase, but only the first letter of Kentish is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Kiddo is an informal word for a youngster, especially a boy.

clue.text: Hamlet's one tragedy originally taking place in university

parts.note: Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark, so he is one of these

indicators.note: originally picks the opening letter of the word tragedy

parts.note: something that is on is happening

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Dane studies a tragedy at college, as he did at Wittenberg.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's one looks like a possessive, but it means 'what Hamlet is one of'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ivy League university in New Jersey is one of America's oldest seats of higher learning.

clue.text: Cheat and cool criminal that Francis

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Cheat and cool criminal that Francis', looks cut short: the anagram of CHEAT COOL works, but 'that Francis' defines nothing and the rest of the definition is missing.
annotationWithheld.clue: Cheat and cool criminal that Francis

clue.text: Self-absorbed type of knight Cassius upset without reason primarily

parts.note: N is the chess notation for knight

indicators.note: without means outside, so the anagram goes around the letter picked from reason
upset means knocked over, so the letters of Cassius are jumbled
primarily picks the first letter of the word reason

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's Cassius is upset for no reason.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside here, not 'lacking'. 'upset' rearranges CASSIUS into ACISSUS, which goes around R.
explanation.definitionFit: The youth of Greek myth fell in love with his own reflection, so his name means a vain person.

clue.text: "And my soul from out that shadow that lies floating on the floor Shall be lifted - !" (Edgar Allen Poe)

definitions.text: "And my soul from out that shadow that lies floating on the floor Shall be lifted - !" (Edgar Allen Poe)

parts.words: "And my soul from out that shadow that lies floating on the floor Shall be lifted - !" (Edgar Allen Poe)
parts.note: the missing word closes the last line of The Raven, the refrain the bird keeps croaking

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: the gap is the raven's one-word refrain, which ends the poem.
explanation.definitionFit: The last line of Poe's The Raven ends with the bird's refrain meaning 'never again'.

clue.text: Moriarty is one overly-proud about intending evil

indicators.note: about places the first piece around the second

parts.note: vain means conceited, overly proud
ill as in ill will, meaning bad intent

explanation.surface: Holmes's arch-enemy is arrogant and plotting harm.
explanation.walkthrough: Professor Moriarty is Sherlock Holmes's arch-enemy.
explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's Professor Moriarty is the criminal mastermind opposing Holmes, the archetypal bad guy.

clue.text: Run into river in which Cadfael might be seen?

definitions.text: in which Cadfael might be seen?

indicators.note: into places the run inside the river

parts.note: the Oder is a river of central Europe
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A medieval monk-detective wades into a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Brother Cadfael, Ellis Peters's sleuth, is a Benedictine monk, so he is seen in a religious order.
explanation.definitionFit: A monastic order, such as the Benedictines, is a body of monks under one rule, which Cadfael belongs to.

clue.text: Scoundrels pinching bottom and butts

indicators.note: pinching means gripping, so the first piece holds the second inside it

parts.note: dogs is an old insult for scoundrels
the end is the bottom of something

explanation.surface: Villains grope someone's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: Butts looks like buttocks, matching the surface, but here it means cigarette ends.
explanation.definitionFit: Butts are the stubs of smoked cigarettes.

clue.text: Country song on listening device that liberal wears

indicators.note: in an across answer, one piece on another is placed after it
wears puts the liberal inside the bug, as if wearing it

parts.note: a bug is a hidden microphone
an aria is a song in opera

explanation.surface: A country song is played on a wire that a liberal wears.
explanation.walkthrough: Country song suggests country music; Country alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Bulgaria is a nation in south-eastern Europe on the Black Sea.

clue.text: Freely-displayed final part of verse in Shakespeare?

indicators.note: in puts the picked letter inside the word for Shakespeare

parts.note: the Bard is Shakespeare's nickname

indicators.note: final part of picks the last letter of the word verse

explanation.surface: The end of a line of verse in Shakespeare is shown openly.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bared is uncovered and openly shown.

clue.text: Heading for Atlanta, pass by university valediction abroad

indicators.note: heading for picks the first letter of the word Atlanta

parts.note: to pass away is to die

explanation.surface: Travelling to Atlanta, someone drives past a college and says goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for farewell is used in English as a goodbye.

clue.text: Feral boy cut by German light infantry

parts.note: to mow is to cut grass
LI is the abbreviation for light infantry

explanation.surface: A wild child is wounded by German foot soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's Jungle Book hero is a boy raised by wolves in the jungle.

clue.text: What might grab your attention in, perhaps, Stoner

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Something in John Williams's novel Stoner catches the eye.
explanation.walkthrough: The run straddles the comma, at the end of perhaps and start of Stoner.
explanation.definitionFit: A whispered call to catch someone's ear quietly.

clue.text: A lie tries rearranging these

indicators.note: rearranging asks for the letters of the preceding words in a new order

explanation.surface: Lying is an attempt to rearrange the facts.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: a lie attempts to rearrange the facts of the world.
explanation.definitionFit: A lie tries to twist the actual facts, the true state of things.

clue.text: Grey and silver poles surrounding head of estuary

parts.note: AG is the chemical symbol for silver

indicators.note: surrounding places the poles on either side of the next piece

parts.note: N and S are the north and south poles

indicators.note: head of picks the first letter of the word estuary

explanation.surface: Grey and silver colours describe a misty river mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: Grey looks like a colour, but it is Anne Brontë's heroine, title of her novel Agnes Grey.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Brontë named her first novel after its governess heroine, whose surname is Grey.

clue.text: Lover of uni enrolled in academic part of the year

parts.note: a don is a university teacher

indicators.note: enrolled in places the university inside the month

parts.note: Jan is January, a part of the year
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A student loves their university during the academic term.
explanation.walkthrough: Academic part of the year suggests a term; academic is the DON and part of the year is JAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary Spanish seducer's name has become a byword for a womaniser.

clue.text: Tenor associated with robberies in The Believers?

parts.note: heists are robberies

explanation.surface: A singer is linked with crimes in a novel called The Believers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Believers is a novel by Zoë Heller, which is the misdirection; the question mark marks the definition as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: People who believe in God are believers, as opposed to atheists.
